You asked me at your wedding why my husband Nikhil looked so tired, and I got angry and walked away. I owe you the truth.
I check his phone every night. I keep his salary in my account "for savings." I choose what he wears to office. I've told him your husband is a bad influence, so he doesn't come to your place anymore.
I always told myself this was love. I worried about him. But when I'm honest, it was fear. Fear that if I didn't hold everything, he'd drift away and I'd have nothing.
At your wedding I saw him standing alone by the wall, checking his phone to see if I needed him. I saw how small his life has become around my rules.
I've made an appointment with a counsellor for myself on Friday. I want to learn to love him without owning him.
Please don't tell anyone yet.
Bhavna

Sarita, you asked me to describe a normal week. Okay. I'm Suraj, and I'll try to be honest.
Monday, I check Priya's phone after dinner. I tell myself it's because I worry. Tuesday, she wants to meet her college friends. I say it's not safe. She stays home. Wednesday, I check her bank app. I handle the money, she has a card for groceries. Thursday, I tell her the blue dress is too much for office. She changes.
She never shouts. She just says "okay" and goes quiet.
I always called it love. Protecting her. But this morning I saw her standing at the window, just looking out, like someone in a small room.
When I really ask myself why I do it, it's fear. If she has her own money and her own friends, maybe she won't need me. Maybe she'll leave.
I don't want her to live in a smaller and smaller life. That's why I'm here. What do I do now?

qa.a: He checks her bank app.

qa.a: Suraj realises it is fear, that if Priya has her own money and friends she might not need Suraj and might leave.

March. He suggested her salary go into their joint account, which only he could log into. "I'm better with money." She agreed. He felt relieved, in control.
May. He told her the new kurta was "too much" for the office party. She changed. He said her friend Pooja was "a bad influence." Sharmila stopped seeing Pooja. Each time, the tight fear in his chest eased a little.
July. At dinner, Jeevan noticed Sharmila hadn't laughed in weeks. Her phone never buzzed anymore. She asked him whether she could buy a book. A book.
He looked at her and felt something cold. He had called it love. But her whole life now fitted inside his rules.
The next morning, while she slept, he looked up a counsellor for himself.

At the insurance office where she'd worked for two years, Sharmila used to be the one who organised birthday lunches. Now, when colleagues asked her to join, she said, "I'll check," and then didn't come.
On Thursday, the team lead asked her to travel to Nashik for a client meeting. Sharmila said, "Can I tell you tomorrow?" She needed to ask Vikas first. She always needed to ask Vikas first: about lunches, about late meetings, about which colleagues she spoke to.
In the washroom, she stood at the sink and realised her hands were shaking. Over a simple work trip.
There were no bruises. Vikas never hit her. So she had never called it anything. But she walked on eggshells every evening, and her world was now her desk, her home, and his rules.
A colleague came in, saw her face and said softly, "Sharmila, are you okay?" For the first time, Sharmila said, "No. Not really."

Dear Noor,
It's been a year since I answered your messages properly. I'm sorry. I want to explain, even though it's hard.
After the wedding, things changed slowly. First I stopped coming to our Sunday lunches because he didn't like them. Then I started asking him before I met anyone. Then before I bought anything. Now I think about how he'll react before I choose what to cook, what to wear, what to say.
He has never hit me, Noor. So for a long time I told myself this wasn't abuse. Just marriage. Just how he is.
But last week I realised I was whispering on the phone with my own mother. In my own home. I walk on eggshells all day.
I'm not asking you to fix anything. I just needed one person outside to know. Could we speak on Thursday at noon, when he's at work? I found a helpline number too. I haven't called yet.
Vandana

Arnab, you asked why I stopped coming to family dinners. I'm Lalremsiami, your sister, and I'm going to try to say it without crying.
It wasn't one big thing. It was small things. He didn't like my friends, so I saw them less. He wanted to know where I was, so I started sending him my location. He said my laugh was embarrassing in public, so I laughed less. Now, before I buy vegetables, I think about what he'll say.
He's never hurt me. There's never been a mark. So I kept telling myself it wasn't abuse. It was just him being particular.
But last month I went to a support group at the women's centre, and a woman there described her week, and it was my week. Exactly.
My world is so small now, Arnab. I'm not asking you to do anything big. Just keep calling me. Please don't stop calling.

Liam and Bao had shared a flat in Dublin for three years before Bao moved in with his girlfriend. Now Liam saw him once a month, if that.
Each time, Liam noticed more. Bao checked his phone every few minutes and texted where he was: "at the pub with Liam," "leaving now," "on the bus." When Liam offered to split the bill, Bao said quietly, "I don't have my card. She keeps it now. It's easier."
He used to laugh loudly. Now he looked at the door a lot.
Liam wanted to say, "Mate, this is not right. Leave." But he'd read that pushing too hard can drive someone back, closer to the person controlling them.
So he said, "I miss you. I'm always around. Pub every second Friday? My treat until you sort the card thing." And, before Bao left: "If you ever need anything, day or night, call me."
Bao nodded, and held on a second too long in the hug.

qa.q: Who keeps Bao's card now?
qa.a: She keeps it now.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling as he noticed the changes in Bao?
qa.a: Liam felt worried and frustrated, wanting to tell Bao to leave but holding back so as not to push him away.

qa.q: What did Liam do that fits a helpful response?
qa.a: He stayed in touch without blame, offered regular meetups and made clear Bao could call him any time.

qa.q: How does Bao seem to feel during the meetup?
qa.a: Bao seems anxious and watchful, checking his phone and the door, and grateful, holding the hug a second too long.

In the small clinic where they both worked as receptionists, Arohi had started noticing things about Tenzin.
She used to come to the staff lunch every Friday. Now she ate alone at her desk, and when Arohi asked, she said she'd forgotten her money again. Her husband handled everything, she said. She texted him before she went to the pharmacy next door, and after she came back. Her phone buzzed whenever she was two minutes late.
Arohi's first impulse was to say, "Tenzin, this isn't normal. You should leave him." She didn't. She'd seen a cousin pushed that way once, and the cousin had cut everyone off.
Instead, on Friday, she brought two tiffins. "I made too much. Eat with me?" They talked about nothing. Before Tenzin went back to her desk, Arohi said, "Whatever you need, anytime, I'm here. No questions."
Tenzin's eyes filled. She nodded, and took the tiffin box back with her.

qa.a: She texted her husband.

I've been thinking about Diwali all week.
You looked so tired. You checked your phone every few minutes and texted Rohit where you were, even when you went to the kitchen. When Ma asked you to come shopping, you said you didn't have money with you, though you've always earned more than me. You didn't laugh once.

Helpline caseworker's note, Tuesday.
Ganga called at 11:40 in the morning, from a colleague's phone at work. She spoke quietly. Her husband monitors her phone and bank account, and his anger has been getting worse. She wants to leave but is afraid.
I explained that the time of leaving is often when the risk is highest, so we plan carefully before any big step.
Together we worked out a few things. She will keep copies of her ID and certificates with her brother Kishore, whom she trusts completely. She'll save the helpline number under a friend's name. She and Kishore agreed on a simple phrase that means "come now." She knows the nearest police station and our local centre's address.
She sounded calmer by the end. "I didn't know there were steps," she said.
We will call her again on Friday at the same time, on the colleague's phone. Kishore has been given our number too.

qa.q: Who will keep copies of Ganga's ID and certificates?
qa.a: Her brother Kishore, whom she trusts completely.

qa.a: Ganga seemed calmer and a little relieved, surprised to learn there were steps she could take.

qa.q: What safety steps did Ganga and the caseworker plan?
qa.a: Keeping documents with Kishore, saving the helpline under another name, a phrase meaning "come now", and knowing the police station and centre.

Wednesday, written at the office, not at home
I did it. At lunch I called the helpline number I'd saved as "Tailor." A calm woman listened for half an hour. She didn't tell me to leave. She said the moment of leaving is often the riskiest, so we would plan first.
She asked who I trust. I said Bhupen, from accounts, who once asked if I was okay and never pushed.
After lunch I told Bhupen, quietly, by the printer. He didn't make a fuss. He just said, "What do you need?" I gave him an envelope with my passport, degree certificate and a copy of my bank papers. He locked it in his drawer.
The helpline gave me the address of a women's support centre. I have an appointment there on Monday.
I'm so scared. But for the first time in two years, I feel like I'm doing something. I'm keeping this diary at work, in my locker.
Neelam
